# wstawki: {INN} {ENEMY} {SIEGE} {BESIEGER} {HUNGRY} {LORD} {HOUSE} {GROOM} {BRIDE} - brak wartosci w migawce swiata = kwestia odpada

column5: Lean in a little. The walls here have more ears than the stable has flies.
Now then. Here's what's been passing over my counter this week.
You paid, so you'll hear it. Mind, I only repeat what others say.
Sit still a moment and I'll give you the news, such as it is.
Talk's cheap, but you've bought the ale, so here's the talk.
I hear everything from behind this counter. Most of it's rubbish. Some of it isn't.
A cup of ale and a mouthful of news - that's the custom here.
Keep your voice down when I tell you this. Not everyone in here is a friend.
Carters, pedlars, a priest or two - they all talk when they drink. Listen.
You want the news? Here it is, fresh as yesterday's bread.
I'm not a gossip, mind. I just have very good ears.
Drink slow and listen close. I won't say it twice.
Funny you should ask. Only last night a man sat right where you are and told me this.
Ale loosens tongues, mine included. Here's what I know.
You've the look of someone who wants to know which way the wind blows. Well.
Between you, me and this barrel, here's how things stand.
Everyone who comes through that door leaves a bit of news behind. Here's this week's pile.
Hold your cup and hold your tongue, and I'll tell you what's been said.
I keep the news like I keep the ale - in the back, for paying folk.
Here's what the road has been saying, for whatever it's worth.
It's been a busy week for talk, if not for coin. Listen to this.
I'll tell you what I told the last fellow, and he went away happy.
Pull your stool closer. The fire's loud and so is the drunk in the corner.
My wife says I talk too much. My customers say I don't talk enough. You decide.
The drovers were full of it last night. Here's what stuck.
You've paid, so I'll pour you news with your ale. No extra charge.
Now listen. Some of this is true, some of it is half true, and I can't tell you which.
News travels by cart, by boat and by bellyache. Here's what arrived.
Here's the latest, and if it turns out wrong, blame the man who told me.
I hear things. It's the one part of this trade that pays nothing and never runs dry.
You look like a sensible sort. Sensible sorts listen. So listen.
Wipe the foam off your lip and I'll tell you a thing or two.
Every traveller wants the same two things - a dry seat and the news. You've the seat.
The well of gossip never runs dry in this house. Here's a bucketful.
Hush now. This is the sort of thing you tell quietly.
There's a lot going on beyond this door. More than most of my customers like.
I'll give it to you straight, the way it was given to me.
A soldier, a smith and a septon walked in last week. Not a jest - here's what they said.
It's not all bad news. Most of it, mind. Not all.
The roads bring trade, and trade brings talk. Here it is.
Ask a keeper for the news and you'll get more than you wanted. Ready?
You'll have heard some of this already, I'd wager. Not all of it, though.
I write nothing down. It's all up here, and here's what's up here.
Talk at this counter has been thick as porridge lately.
Settle in. There's a fair bit to tell.
If anyone asks, you heard this from a pedlar, not from me.
I'll trade you news for coin any day. Better trade than most I make.
Here's the gist of it, without the shouting and the spilled ale.
This came in with the last carters, and they had it from the ferrymen.
One cup, one tale. That's my rule, and I'm generous with it.
You've an honest face. Mostly. Here's what's being said.
Stories come in with muddy boots and leave with full bellies. Here's one or two.
I've been keeping this one for a customer who'd appreciate it.
Some news is worth a copper. Some is worth a silver. This is somewhere in between.
Lean on the counter, it's sturdier than it looks. Now.
Let me tell you what the travellers have been whispering.
I hear more than a maester and remember more than a priest. Here goes.
All right. Here's what's been talked over in this room since the last new moon.
My father kept this house before me, and he said: listen more than you pour. So I listened.
Before the fiddler starts up again, here's the news.
Don't look round. Just listen.
Sit, sip, listen. In that order.
The world's gone mad again. Here's the latest proof.
I'll tell you, but you'll want another cup after.
Everyone's been on about the same few things. Here they are.
They say a keeper knows everything. I don't. But I know this.
You paid fair, so you get it fair. Here's the talk.
Plenty of folk through here this week, and every one with a tale.
Let's see. Where shall I start?
Now that you've a cup in your hand, here's what goes with it.
You can trust what I tell you as far as you can trust anyone who tells me things.
The hearth hears it first, and I hear it second. Here's what the hearth heard.
Mark this, but don't repeat it too loud.
It's a strange season. Here's how strange.
It's the same old talk, with a few new turns. Listen.
A merchant came in soaked to the bone and paid with good silver. He also talked.
Quiet now, there's a fellow by the window I don't trust.
You'll want to hear this, I think.
Here's what I've gathered, like a squirrel with nuts.
Let me fill your cup and your ears both.
This is how the wind's blowing, near as I can tell.
I don't take sides, I take coin. But I hear what both sides say.
Two pilgrims and a tinker were here till dawn. They didn't stop talking once.
I'll tell you what I know, and you'll forget where you heard it.
Right then. The news, as it was told to me.
News is like stew - better if it's been stirred a while. This has been well stirred.
Ears open, cup full. Good. Here it is.
I could tell you about the weather. Or I could tell you this.
They all talk to me. I'm like a priest with a tap.
Now, you didn't hear any of this from me, understand?
That's good ale, that. And here's some good talk to go with it.
Lean closer, friend. Here's what folk are saying.
Folk talk more when it rains. And it's rained a lot this week.
Here's what's crossed my counter since you were last this way, or since anyone was.
I'll tell you what everyone's talking about, and a bit that only I know.
Since you're buying, I'm telling.
That's all I've got, and more than I should have said.
And you didn't hear any of it from me.
Now drink up before it goes warm.
That's the talk. Make of it what you will.
Mind how you go with that. Words have a way of coming back.
If any of that turns out wrong, I'll stand you a free cup. Probably.
That's the lot. Another cup might shake loose a bit more.
Don't go repeating that in front of the wrong people.
Make good use of it, and remember where you heard it. Or better, don't.
That's all for now. My mouth's dry from telling it.
There. Now you know as much as I do, gods help you.
Keep that under your hat.
Use it wisely, friend.
And that's how the world turns, from where I'm standing.
Your cup's empty. So's my head, for the moment.
I've told you all I know and a bit I don't.
Be careful on the road, with all that going on.
Well, that's the news. The ale's better than the news, at least.
More I can't say. More I don't know.
That'll do for one cup, I think.
That's the story. I'd not bet my house on it, mind.
And if you hear different, come back and tell me.
Gods know what tomorrow brings. That's today.
Now go easy. Half of that will be wrong by next week.
That's it. The rest is just drunks and weather.
Go on, drink. News goes down easier with ale.
Remember, I'm only the keeper. I just pour.
You'll be wanting another, I'd guess.
That's the news. Don't shoot the man who pours it.
Mind, it's only what folk say. Folk say a lot.
I'll hear more by morning, if you're staying.
Take that with a pinch of salt. Or a cup of ale.
Now, enough of that. Your ale's going flat.
Gods keep you on the road, with all that afoot.
And that's the end of it, unless someone walks in with more.
Lot of trouble about, isn't there? Drink up.
That's my news. Now let's talk about your tab.
That'll set you thinking, I expect.
If you hear anything worth knowing on the road, bring it back. I trade.
That's all the gossip fit for a paying guest.
I'll leave it there. The fire wants feeding.
No more talk till you're on your second cup.
There's always more, but that's the meat of it.
That's what they're saying. What they're thinking, gods only know.
And now I've said too much. Again.
So there it is. Strange times.
I've nothing more, unless you want to hear about my bad knee.
That's the sum of it. Your coin, your cup, your business.
Not a word of that to anyone in a cloak and a badge.
And that's why I never leave this inn.
You heard it here first. Unless you didn't.
I don't know what it all means. I just pass it along.
Use it or lose it, as my old mother said.
That's my lot. Someone else's turn to talk.
Make what you can of it. I've made nothing of it yet.
Right. Back to work for me.
Keep your eyes open out there.
That's the news from this side of the hearth.
Sleep on it, if you're sleeping here.
The rest is rumour on top of rumour.
I'll pour another if you want more.
And that's as much as anybody knows.
Say a prayer for the lot of them, I would.
I'll not say more with the door open.
That'll keep you company on the road.
You can thank me by not mentioning my name.
Enough. Drink.
There's your news, warm from the hearth.
I'm out of tales and you're out of ale. Funny how that works.
That's the shape of it. The details, ask somebody drunker.
I've talked myself hoarse. Pass me that jug.
Whatever comes of it, the ale will still be here.
That's that, then.
Gods, listen to me. Like an old woman at a well.
More than that, you'd have to ask the crows.
I'll be hearing more by the next new moon, never fear.
And now you know why I keep an axe under the counter.
Don't let it spoil your drink.
Make your plans accordingly, friend.
That's the talk of the house. The house thanks you for your custom.
I've given you your coin's worth, I'd say.
The world's in a hurry these days. Better to sit and drink.
That's what came through that door. What goes out it is your business.
Some of that will make you rich. Some of it will get you hanged. Choose well.
Remember, you got it cheap.
And that's the news, keep it warm.
Better you hear it here than find out on the road.
I've said my piece.
That's the lot, unless you're buying another.
I'd stay off the main roads, if I were you. Just a thought.
That's how the dice have fallen, for now.
Another cup? The second one tells more.
There. I feel lighter for saying it.
The rest can wait till morning.
And mind you don't spill it - the ale, I mean. The news you can spill all you like.
That's the long and the short of it.
More than that I won't swear to.
There it is. Like it or not.
That's what the road told me. The road's a liar, sometimes.
And now we both know. Gods help us.
Mind the step on your way out. Everyone trips on it.
Have another cup and forget half of it, that's my advice.
That's all the news that's fit to tell, and some that isn't.
There you are. Mind the foam, it's the best part.
One ale, poured honest. Now, about the news.
Here. Drink, and I'll talk.
Good choice. That barrel's the fresh one.
Here's your cup. The news comes with the second swallow.
Poured to the brim, which is more than most keepers do.
There. Now, where to begin?
Your ale, friend. Sit and I'll tell you what I know.
That'll warm you. Now, the talk.
A fair cup for a fair coin. And a tale on top.
There's your drink. Mind, it's strong. So is the news.
Ale for the traveller. Now lean in.
Here you go. I'll tell you while you drink.
Fresh from the cask. Listen while it's cold.
One ale. And a mouthful of news to wash down with it.
There. Now don't gulp, I talk slow.
I'll give you a cup and the gossip both. Here.
Drink up. The talk's been lively this week.
A full cup. Your health. Now here's the word.
There's your ale, and here's the latest.
Pour, pour, there. Now we can talk.
Ale's poured, ears ready? Good.
Here, catch. Just jesting - here.
Brown and honest, like my mother. Drink.
Here's your drink. The news is on the house.
There you are. Now, did you hear about this?
Get that down you. Then we'll talk.
A cup for you, and a word or two. Here.
Mind it's hot - no, it's ale, it's not hot. Long day. Here.
There's your cup. Sit, and I'll tell you the talk.
M: My cart lost a wheel two miles back. || F: And you walked the rest? || M: I rolled the cart. Slowly. || F: That explains the state of you.
F: The baker's girl is with child again. || M: Again? Who's the father? || F: She says it's the miller. The miller says it's the weather. || M: Well, it has been a warm spring.
M: I swear this bench was longer last year. || M: You were thinner last year. || M: I was poorer last year. || M: Same thing, near enough.
F: Has anyone seen my brother? He went to sell a goat. || M: Three days ago? || F: Four. || M: Then either the goat sold him, or he's drinking the price somewhere.
M: There's a septon on the road preaching against ale. || F: In an inn? || M: Outside the inn. He comes in after, for a cup. || F: A man of principle, then.
F: My husband wants to buy a second cow. || M: Sounds sensible. || F: We haven't the grass for the first one. || M: Ah. Then he wants a second field first.
M: Have you ever seen the sea? || M: Once. Big. Wet. Salty. || M: That's all? || M: What else is there? It doesn't change.
F: The pedlar sold me a ribbon that he swore was silk. || M: Was it? || F: It came apart in the rain. || M: Then it was silk-coloured.
M: My father lived to seventy. || M: What was his secret? || M: Never married, never fought, never paid a toll he could walk round. || M: Then how were you born? || M: That's a long story.
F: I've walked all day and my feet are crying. || F: Take your shoes off. || F: Here? || F: Nobody here will mind. Look at them. || F: Fair point.
M: The keeper's dog stole my sausage. || M: That dog is the best fed creature for fifty miles. || M: Or a hundred. || M: Better fed than the keeper, I'd wager.
M: I had a dream I was a lord. || F: And? || M: Everyone wanted something from me. I woke up glad to be poor. || F: That's the only dream I've heard that makes sense.
F: My grandmother could tell the weather from her knees. || M: Mine could tell it from the sky. || F: Hers was more reliable. || M: Mine looked up more often.
M: They put up a new toll stone by the old bridge. || M: Who did? || M: The lord's steward. || M: And who put up the bridge? || M: Our grandfathers. Funny how that works.
F: Did you hear the singer last night? || M: Hear him? I paid him to stop. || F: He took the coin? || M: And then started a new song. Cleverest man in the room.
M: I've been on this road since I was twelve. || M: And where's it got you? || M: Here. With you. || M: Then the road's had a hard life too.
F: The wool price is up. || M: Good for you, you keep sheep. || F: Bad for me, I buy cloth. || M: Then sell to yourself.
M: I met a man who said he was a knight. || M: Was he? || M: He had a sword and no horse. || M: Then he was half a knight. The cheaper half.
F: My boy wants to be a soldier. || M: Let him. || F: He's nine. || M: Let him when he's ten, then.
M: I've a cousin who works in a lord's kitchen. || M: Eats well? || M: Eats scraps. But such scraps. || M: I'd marry for those scraps.
F: This stew has a finger in it. || M: A finger? || F: A carrot. Shaped like a finger. || M: Gods, woman, don't do that to a man.
M: My wife's cooking has gone downhill. || M: Since when? || M: Since I told her it was good. || M: Never praise. They stop trying.
F: Never trust a man who doesn't drink. || M: Why not? || F: He's remembering everything. || M: I'll have another, then.
M: There's a hermit up by the old tower. || F: What does he do? || M: Nothing. Sits. Talks to crows. || F: Sounds restful.
M: I lost at dice again. || M: How much? || M: My good boots. || M: Is that why you're barefoot? || M: No, that was the bet before.
F: The wise woman says to boil nettles for a cough. || M: Does it work? || F: You stop coughing because you're busy complaining about the taste.
M: My mule bit the steward. || M: Good mule. || M: The steward fined me. || M: Worth every copper.
F: My sister married a man from the next valley. || M: Is he good to her? || F: He's quiet, he works, he doesn't drink. || M: Then he's a strange one.
M: The roads are full of beggars this year. || M: Every year. || M: More this year. || M: You say that every year too.
M: I've a scar from a bear. || F: Show us. || M: It's in a delicate place. || F: Then it was a delicate bear.
F: The new priest is young. || F: How young? || F: He blushed when old Bessa confessed. || F: Everybody blushes when old Bessa confesses.
M: A raven flew in through the window last week. || M: Messages? || M: No, just a raven. Ate my bread. || M: Then it was a message. It said you were careless.
M: I heard you can buy a man's debt and make him work it off. || M: You can. || M: Isn't that slavery? || M: Lords call it husbandry.
F: My man snores like a bellows. || F: Mine too. || F: How do you sleep? || F: I sleep in the barn. The cows are quieter.
M: Ever eaten a peacock? || M: Ever eaten a what? || M: Big bird. Lords eat them. || M: Lords will eat anything if it's expensive.
F: I've been weaving since dawn. || M: Sell much? || F: Sold one blanket to a man who used it as a saddle. || M: Then it's a good blanket.
M: The miller cheats on weight. || M: All millers cheat on weight. || M: This one cheats twice. || M: Then he's twice the miller.
M: Saw a two-headed snake once. || F: And did it bite you? || M: Couldn't decide which head would do it. || F: Like a council of lords.
F: My daughter's sweet on the smith's boy. || M: Good trade, smithing. || F: He's a terrible smith. || M: Then she's sweet on him for other reasons.
M: The well water tastes of iron. || M: Good for the blood, they say. || M: Who says? || M: The man who sells the water.
M: My brother came back from the city. || M: Changed? || M: Talks fancy and won't muck out the pigs. || M: Then he's ruined. Send him back.
F: They say a maid saw a ghost in the old mill. || M: What did it look like? || F: The old miller. || M: Then it's not a ghost, he's just been hiding from his creditors.
M: I should have been a priest. || M: Why? || M: They get fed and nobody hits them. || M: Somebody always hits a priest eventually.
M: How far to the next town? || M: Two days on foot. || M: And on a horse? || M: Two days, if it's your horse. One if it's someone else's.
F: These stools are terrible. || M: They're meant to be. || F: Why? || M: So you don't fall asleep and stop buying.
M: I've seen a knight eat a whole goose. || M: By himself? || M: He offered me a wing. Then thought better of it. || M: That's knights for you.
F: I keep bees. || M: Do they sting? || F: Only the ones who deserve it. || M: Then you'll have to teach me which ones I am.
M: They've raised the market fee again. || F: Why? || M: The lord's daughter is getting married. || F: So we pay for her wedding? || M: We always do.
M: I once carried a letter for a lord. || M: What did it say? || M: Couldn't read it. || M: Then you're the best messenger a lord could want.
F: My feet are wet, my purse is empty, and my husband is in the next village. || M: Two out of three bad. || F: Which is the good one? || M: Up to you.
M: I've a riddle. What has teeth but never eats? || M: A comb. || M: Damn. Everybody knows that one. || M: Get a new riddle.
M: I traded my sword for a pig. || F: Good trade? || M: The pig's been more use. || F: And it's easier to clean.
F: The weaver down the lane says the gods are angry. || M: About what? || F: She didn't say. Probably about her prices.
M: My old captain used to say: never volunteer. || M: Did you listen? || M: I volunteered to buy the next round. || M: Then you didn't.
M: Ever seen a lord laugh? || M: Once. At a funeral. || M: Whose? || M: His brother's. Inheritance, you see.
F: My girl can count to a thousand. || M: Clever. || F: Only takes her all morning. || M: Still cleverer than a steward.
M: I'm off to the mountains to look for silver. || M: You'll find rocks. || M: Rocks with silver in them. || M: Rocks with rocks in them, more like.
M: The keeper's brew is better this year. || M: Same barrels. || M: Different water. || M: Different keeper's wife. She makes it now.
F: Somebody stole my washing off the line. || F: All of it? || F: Only my husband's breeches. || F: Then somebody's welcome to them.
M: You owe me two coppers. || M: I paid you back. || M: When? || M: In spirit. || M: Spirit doesn't buy ale.
M: My horse is older than my wife. || M: Better tempered? || M: Better looking. Don't tell her.
F: The tinker mended my pot. || M: And did it hold? || F: Held water for a day. Then held soup for a minute. || M: Tinker's work.
M: If I were a lord I'd ban toll roads. || M: If you were a lord you'd own the toll roads. || M: Then I'd ban the other ones.
M: There's good fishing up the river. || M: Is there? || M: There was. Before I told everyone. || M: Then keep your mouth shut next time.
F: My mother says a woman should never travel alone. || M: And here you are. || F: I'm not alone. I've my knife. || M: Fair company.
M: I knew a man who could drink a whole cask. || M: What happened to him? || M: They buried him in it. Fitting.
M: My son can read. || M: Who taught him? || M: The septon, for a pig. || M: And what does he read? || M: The pig's ear tag, mostly.
F: I'm going to the market to sell eggs. || M: How many? || F: Three. The hen's lazy. || M: Then eat them and save the walk.
M: Ever wonder what lords talk about? || M: Money and marriages. || M: Same as us. || M: Bigger numbers.
M: They took my son for the levy. || F: Did they pay? || M: They paid with a promise. || F: Promises don't plough.
M: Soldiers came through yesterday. Asked for bread. || M: Did you give it? || M: They didn't ask twice. || M: They never do.
F: They're saying {ENEMY} is marching. || M: They're always marching somewhere. || F: This time towards us. || M: Then pour another, quick.
M: Which way is the war? || M: Every way. || M: That's no help. || M: That's the truth.
M: My lord says the war will be short. || M: Which lord said that? || M: Mine. || M: The last lord who said that is in a ditch.
F: Every man between fifteen and fifty has been called. || F: What about the old ones? || F: They're next, if it goes on. || F: Then we'll be bringing the harvest in ourselves.
M: I sold three horses to the army this week. || M: Good price? || M: They paid. Half. || M: Better half than none.
M: The fighting with {ENEMY} is getting closer. || F: How close? || M: Close enough that the crows are fat. || F: Gods keep us.
F: My man went to fight and sent back a letter. || M: What did it say? || F: Couldn't read it. Got the priest to read it. || M: And? || F: He wants his good boots.
M: Who started this war anyway? || M: Lords. || M: Which lords? || M: All of them. And we finish it.
M: They're paying soldiers in copper now. || M: Copper? || M: The silver's gone to the swords. || M: And the swords are gone to the crows.
F: The war's taken every cart in the village. || M: How do you get to market? || F: We don't. We eat what we grow. || M: Then the war's done you a favour, in a way.
M: No soldiers on the roads this month. || F: Long may it last. || M: It won't. || F: Then enjoy it while it does.
F: My boy came home from the levy. Peace, they said. || M: Is he whole? || F: Whole and lazy. Sleeps till noon. || M: That's peace for you.
M: The lords have made peace. || M: For how long? || M: Till the next harvest, I'd guess. || M: Then plant quickly.
M: Quiet times. Trade's picking up. || M: For you, maybe. || M: For everyone. || M: For the tax collectors, certainly.
F: It's cold enough to freeze the words in your mouth. || M: Then stop talking. || F: You first.
M: Frost on the inside of the shutters this morning. || M: That's winter. || M: That's poverty. Winter's just the excuse.
F: My chickens won't lay. || M: Too cold. || F: I told them that. Didn't help.
M: Snow's closed the high pass. || M: How long for? || M: Till the thaw. || M: And when's the thaw? || M: Ask the gods. They're not answering.
M: Firewood costs more than food now. || F: So eat the firewood. || M: I tried. Splinters.
F: My grandmother says this winter will be long. || M: She says every winter will be long. || F: And she's never wrong. || M: Well, she's old. She's had practice.
M: The river's frozen solid. || M: Good. We can walk to the other side. || M: What's on the other side? || M: The same frozen nothing. But a change of view.
M: They've put {SIEGE} under siege. || M: Who has? || M: {BESIEGER}, they say. || M: Then the price of grain's going up again.
F: My sister lives in {SIEGE}. || M: Under siege? || F: She'll have eaten the cat by now. || M: Better the cat than the cat eating her.
M: Siege at {SIEGE}. Trebuchets and all. || M: How long can they last? || M: As long as the bread does. || M: Then not long.
M: I was meant to sell wool in {SIEGE}. || M: Bad luck. || M: Bad luck for the wool. It'll rot. || M: Bad luck for the people inside too.
F: What happens when a town falls? || M: You don't want to know. || F: I do. || M: Then you'll not sleep tonight.
M: The army round {SIEGE} needs feeding. || M: So? || M: So their foragers are taking everything for miles. || M: Then lock your barn.
M: They say the walls at {SIEGE} are old but thick. || M: Thick walls, thin bread. || M: That's how sieges go.
F: There's no bread in {HUNGRY}. || M: None at all? || F: They're eating the seed grain. || M: Then there'll be none next year either.
M: Folk from {HUNGRY} were begging at the gate today. || M: Did you give anything? || M: What could I give? I've three mouths of my own.
